904.title: Las Casas
904.hook: a Spanish colonist priest in the Americas turns against conquest and defends indigenous people
904.howItsDone: Las Casas is remembered by Catholics, and especially by Dominicans and by Christians working for justice in Latin America, as a defender of indigenous peoples; his writings are still read in debates about conquest and human rights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tikhon of Zadonsk, the bishop who bowed instead of striking back. Your line was all is from God. What did your ordinary object teach you? Day nine hundred four.

A priest sits down to prepare a sermon. He is also a landholder on a Caribbean island, with indigenous Taíno people forced to work his land. He opens the book of Sirach, sometimes called Ecclesiasticus, one of the books Catholic and Orthodox Christians count in the Old Testament, and reads a passage about offerings made from what was taken unjustly. The bread of the needy, it says, is their life, and whoever takes it from them sheds blood. He stops. He can't preach on it and keep living as he lives. So he does what his neighbors won't. He gives his laborers up. Today: Las Casas.

Bartolomé de las Casas came to the Americas as a Spanish settler, in the wave that followed Columbus. Under the system the Spanish called the encomienda, settlers were granted indigenous people to work for them, in theory to be protected and taught the faith, in practice often worked without mercy. Las Casas took part in it, and was even ordained a priest while still holding his grant. Before his own turn, Dominican friars in the islands had already spoken up. One of them, Antonio de Montesinos, preached a sermon to the colonists asking, in effect: are these not human beings? Do they not have souls? Are you not bound to love them as yourselves? The colonists were furious. Las Casas knew that challenge, and later came his reading of Sirach. He gave up his grant, years later joined the Dominicans, and spent the rest of his life arguing, in pamphlets, in books and before the Spanish court, that the native peoples were free human beings, and that conquest and forced labor were sins. He wrote a searing account of the destruction of the Indies, and he debated a scholar who defended the conquest. Our line gathers up what he argued: they are our brothers. Jesus says it in Matthew: "all ye are brethren." There's a hard part, and it belongs in the story. Early on, Las Casas suggested bringing enslaved Africans to spare the native people. Later he wrote that he regretted it, and that the enslavement of Africans was just as unjust. Even a defender of the oppressed had to unlearn something. His story is honored by Catholics and studied far beyond the church.

Here's the practice: speak for someone who is exploited. Sit, and bring to mind someone whose work you rely on and rarely see: the person who picked your food, sewed your clothes, cleaned the building. Hold them for a moment as a brother or sister, with a face and a name you don't know. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and ask what one thing you could say or do for them. The bell holds the time.
Las Casas. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish settler and priest who gave up his grant of indigenous laborers and spent his life defending native peoples against conquest.
Your line: they are our brothers. Today, say one thing out loud, to a store, a friend or a group, on behalf of someone whose work is unseen or unfairly paid. Day nine hundred four.

905.title: Guadalupe (1531)
905.hook: Catholics tell of Mary appearing to Juan Diego, an indigenous man, near Mexico City
905.howItsDone: Catholics in Mexico and beyond keep the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe with processions, songs and Mass, and pilgrims visit her basilica at Tepeyac to see the tilma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Las Casas, the settler priest who gave up his laborers. Your line was they are our brothers. Did you speak up for someone unseen? Day nine hundred five.

A man takes the long way around a hill on purpose. His uncle is dying, he's running for a priest, and he doesn't want to be stopped. On this hill, the story goes, a lady has been speaking to him, sending him with messages to the bishop, and he has failed to bring back the sign the bishop wants. He's embarrassed and he's in a hurry. So he goes around. And she comes down the hill and meets him on the other path anyway. Today: Guadalupe.

This is the story Catholics tell of Our Lady of Guadalupe, told in one old account in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. The man is Juan Diego, an indigenous convert living in the years just after the Spanish conquest of Mexico. On the hill of Tepeyac, near what is now Mexico City, a lady appears to him, speaks to him in his own language, and asks that a church be built there. He goes to the bishop. The bishop, cautious, asks for a sign. Then comes the uncle's illness, and the detour, and the meeting on the other path. What she says to him there has become our line. In the story, she tells him not to be troubled or afraid, and asks: am I not here, I who am your mother? Are you not in my care? She tells him his uncle is already healed. Then she sends him up the hill to gather flowers, in a season when nothing should be blooming. He carries roses down in his cloak, his tilma, and opens it before the bishop. The roses tumble out, and on the cloth, the story says, is her image: a young woman with dark skin, in a mantle of stars, standing on the moon. Notice who the story honors. Not the bishop, not the conquerors. An indigenous man the powerful didn't believe. It sounds like Mary's own song in Luke: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree." The cloak hangs today in her basilica in Mexico City, and the Catholic Church honors Juan Diego as a saint. This is a Catholic devotion. Other Christians honor Mary in different ways, and some do not accept apparitions at all.

Here's the practice: honor a poor person's witness. Sit, and remember someone with little power or money whose word you, or others, didn't take seriously at first: a child, a stranger, a worker, an elder. Hold what they actually said. If you pray, you can pray for them, or with Mary's words from Luke, he hath put down the mighty from their seats. If you don't, simply give their witness its full weight now. The bell holds the time.
Guadalupe. Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mary as Catholics tell of her appearing to Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, leaving her image on his cloak.
Your line: am I not here? Today, when someone overlooked tries to tell you something, stop, turn toward them, and let them finish. Day nine hundred five.

what a scholar hears: a story preserved in Nahuatl in which the powerless man is believed over the bishop, echoing Mary's song in Luke.

906.title: Martin de Porres
906.hook: a mixed-race Dominican brother in Lima who cared for the sick, poor and animals
906.howItsDone: Catholics in Peru and beyond keep the feast of Saint Martin de Porres, and he is pictured with a broom; some parishes and charities named for him care for the sick, the poor or animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guadalupe, and a lady who met Juan Diego on the other path. Your line was am I not here? Did you stop and let someone overlooked finish? Day nine hundred six.

A broom. Not a crown, not a book, not a sword. In paintings and statues of one saint from Peru, that's what he holds: a plain broom, the kind you'd find in any closet. Sometimes there's a dog, a cat and a mouse at his feet, eating from the same dish. He was a man the law of his day kept at the bottom of the ladder, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black mother, and he spent his life at the jobs nobody wanted. Today: Martin de Porres.

Martin was born in Lima, in colonial Peru. His father, a Spaniard, was slow to acknowledge him. His mother had been enslaved and was freed. As a boy Martin was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon, which in those days meant cutting hair, setting bones, bleeding fevers and mixing herbs. Then he knocked at the door of the Dominican friars. Because of his race, the rules of the time didn't allow him to enter as a full member. So he came in as a helper, doing the lowest work in the house: sweeping, laundry, caring for the sick. Only later was he allowed to make vows as a lay brother. He never stopped sweeping. That's our line: the broom saint. Martin ran the friary's infirmary and treated the sick of the city too, rich and poor, Spanish, African and indigenous. He begged for food and money for those who had none. Stories gathered around him: of healings, of being in two places at once, and of animals. One tells how mice were raiding the friary, and instead of poisoning them, Martin led them out to the garden and promised to feed them there if they'd stay out of the linen. Another tells that when the friary fell into debt, he offered to be sold as a slave to pay it. Whether every story happened as told, they show what people saw in him. His life reads like Jesus's words in Matthew: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." And the psalm that says: "his tender mercies are over all his works." All his works, including the mice. The Catholic Church honors Martin as a saint.

Here's the practice: care for an animal. If there's an animal near you, a pet, a bird at the window, even an ant on the floor, sit and watch it with full attention, the way Martin would. Notice what it needs. If there isn't one, remember an animal you've known, and what caring for it was like. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, with the psalm's words, his tender mercies are over all his works. If you don't, simply watch, and be kind. The bell holds the time.
Dominican. The order of friars Martin de Porres joined as a lay brother, sweeping floors and caring for the sick and poor of Lima.
Your line: the broom saint. Today, do one job nobody wants, quietly, without being asked, and leave a little food or water out for some creature. Day nine hundred six.

907.title: Kateri Tekakwitha
907.hook: a Mohawk and Algonquin woman who became a Christian and prayed in the woods
907.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States and Canada visit shrines connected with Kateri Tekakwitha and ask her prayers, and some Indigenous Catholic communities keep her feast day with their own songs and customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin de Porres, the Dominican brother in Lima who swept floors and cared for the sick, the poor and the animals. Your line was the broom saint. What small, plain job did you do with care? Day nine hundred seven.

A small cross, cut with a knife into the bark of a tree. The old accounts of her life say she made crosses like that along the paths she walked, and stopped at them to pray. No chapel. No candles. Snow on the ground some of the year, the river close by, and a woman kneeling in the woods with a scarred face and weak eyes. Her father was Mohawk. Her mother was Algonquin, and a Christian. The Jesuits who knew her wrote her story down. Catholics today call her a saint. Today: Kateri Tekakwitha.

Her story comes to us mostly through two Jesuit priests who knew her and wrote her life. So we hear her through their eyes, and they were writing to praise her. Hold that gently as you listen. The accounts say that as a child she survived smallpox, which left her face marked and her eyesight poor. Her parents died of the same sickness. She grew up with relatives in a Mohawk village, and when Jesuit missionaries came, she listened. She asked for baptism and took the name Kateri, a form of Catherine. The accounts say it cost her. Some in the village mocked her and pressured her to marry. So she left, and went to a Christian village near Montreal, where others like her lived. There, the accounts say, she prayed early and long, fasted hard, cared for the sick, and spent hours in the forest. She once set up a kind of woodland chapel, a cross by a stream. She died young. Tradition says her last words were: Jesus, I love you. And her companions said that after she died, the scars on her face faded. Mark's Gospel tells of Jesus doing something close to what she did: "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Her title, the lily of the Mohawks, came from Christians who honored her. Some Indigenous Catholics hold her close as one of their own. Some Indigenous people remember the missions as part of a much harder story of land and loss. Both memories are real, and her life sits inside both.
screen: `TOLD BY THE JESUITS WHO KNEW HER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray outdoors, or simply sit outdoors. If you can step outside, do: a yard, a balcony, a doorstep, a window opened wide. Find one living thing, a tree, a patch of grass, a weed in a crack. Let it be your marker, the way her crosses in the bark were hers. Then be still with it. If you pray, you can pray there in your own words, or with the Lord's Prayer. If you don't, just listen to whatever is outside. The bell holds the time.
Kateri Tekakwitha. A Mohawk and Algonquin woman who was baptized, left home for a Christian village, and prayed in the woods. Catholics honor her as a saint.
Your line: the lily of the mohawks. Today, mark one spot outside, a tree, a corner, a step, and pause there for one breath each time you pass. Day nine hundred seven.

908.title: Matteo Ricci
908.hook: a Jesuit in China who dressed as a scholar and made friends through maps and clocks
908.howItsDone: Christians who work across cultures often read Ricci's life as a lesson in learning a language and a culture before speaking, and Catholics in China and Italy remember him in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kateri Tekakwitha, praying at a cross cut into the bark of a tree. Your line was the lily of the Mohawks. Did you find a spot outside to pause? Day nine hundred eight.

Visitors keep crowding into one house in a Chinese city. They've come to see a map of the whole world, drawn in Chinese characters, hanging on the wall, and to hear a mechanical clock tick and strike the hour. The man who brought them is an Italian, in the robes of a Chinese scholar, speaking Chinese and quoting the Chinese classics. He has come to talk about Christ. But he has decided he won't start there. He'll start with friendship, and with what his hosts already love: learning. Today: Matteo Ricci.

Matteo Ricci was a Jesuit priest, the order of Ignatius and Francis Xavier you met earlier in this block. He went to China, and the accounts say he first dressed the way Buddhist monks did, thinking that was how religious teachers looked there. Then he learned that the teachers his hosts looked up to were the scholars, the readers of Confucius. So he changed his clothes, and more than his clothes. He studied the classics until he could quote them, and took a Chinese name. He made his world map in Chinese, and he worked with a Chinese scholar named Xu Guangqi to put a Greek geometry book into Chinese. Xu was baptized too. Ricci also wrote a little book on friendship, a collection of sayings about what a friend is, in Chinese, for Chinese readers. And he wrote about God using words and ideas his readers already had, arguing that the old Chinese classics already knew of a Lord of Heaven. Paul said something like it about his own work: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." Not everyone agreed with Ricci. After his death, Catholics argued long and hard over how far that kind of meeting could go, especially over honoring ancestors. Some saw wise respect. Some saw too much given away. But his starting point is the line for today. Jesus says to his disciples in John's Gospel: "I have called you friends." Ricci tried to begin there.
screen: `A MAP, A CLOCK, A GEOMETRY BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about another culture, starting from friendship. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you know whose family, language or country is different from yours. What do they love? A food, a festival, a kind of music, a saying their grandmother used? Pick one thing you've never asked them about. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. If you don't, just wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Matteo Ricci. An Italian Jesuit in China who took a Chinese name, wore a scholar's robes, made a world map and a book on friendship, and tried to speak of God in his hosts' own words.
Your line: friendship first. Today, ask that person the one question you picked, and listen to the whole answer before you say anything about yourself. Day nine hundred eight.

909.title: Japan's hidden Christians
909.hook: after persecution, Japanese Christians kept their faith in secret for generations, with no priests
909.howItsDone: Catholics in Japan remember the hidden Christians and the martyrs, and pilgrims visit the old hidden Christian villages and churches around Nagasaki.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matteo Ricci, in a scholar's robes in China. Your line was friendship first. What did you hear when you asked your question and listened? Day nine hundred nine.

Any official walking into this Japanese farmhouse would see a Buddhist home. On the family altar, a small white statue of Kannon, the Buddhist figure of mercy, holds a child. But the family knows who she really is to them. When the doors are shut, they call her Mary. Behind a cupboard there might be a scrap of cloth, a medal, a prayer that has never been written down. For generations, there were no priests, no churches, and the faith was against the law. And still, somehow, it was kept. Today: Japan's hidden Christians.

You met Francis Xavier sailing to Japan earlier in this block. The faith he and others brought grew, and then Japan's rulers turned against it. Churches were torn down, missionaries expelled, and Christians who wouldn't give up their faith were killed. Officials made people step on an image of Christ or Mary to prove they weren't Christian. Some Christians stepped, and grieved over it afterward. And some villages went underground. They became the hidden Christians, kakure kirishitan in Japanese. With no priests, ordinary people led. One person in a village might be the baptizer, pouring water on each newborn with the words they'd been taught. Another kept the calendar of feasts. Their prayers, called orasho, were learned by heart and passed down from parent to child, mostly by word of mouth, until some of the Latin and Portuguese words wore smooth, like stones in a river, and the people saying them no longer knew exactly what they meant. They kept saying them anyway. Jesus told his followers to "pray to thy Father which is in secret". These families kept that secret room for generations. When Catholic priests came back to Japan, tradition tells of villagers walking into a new church in Nagasaki, and a woman whispering to the priest that their hearts were the same as his. Some hidden communities joined the Catholic Church again. Others kept their own ways, which they had guarded so long. Both were choices about the same thing: what had been kept.
screen: `OUR HEARTS ARE THE SAME AS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small practice to keep faithfully, something tiny enough that nobody would notice it: one line you say on waking, one breath before you eat, a moment at the window at night. Choose it now. Then do it once, here, slowly, as if you were handing it down to someone who will keep it after you. If you pray, you can make it a prayer you already know by heart. If you don't, make it a pause. The bell holds the time.
kakure kirishitan. Japanese for hidden Christians, the families who kept their faith in secret for generations with no priests, through baptisms and prayers learned by heart.
Your line: hidden, but kept. Today, keep the small practice you chose, quietly, at least once more, with nobody watching. Day nine hundred nine.

910.title: Korea's lay founders (1784)
910.hook: Korean scholars read Christian books and founded their own church before any priest arrived
910.howItsDone: Catholics in Korea honor their founders and martyrs, visit shrines connected with them, and point to the church's lay beginnings as part of who they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japan's kakure kirishitan, keeping prayers by heart with no priests. Your line was hidden, but kept. Did you keep your small practice with nobody watching? Day nine hundred ten.

A handful of Korean scholars sit together over a pile of books. They are Confucian men, trained to read closely and argue carefully, and these books have come to them from Beijing, written in classical Chinese, the language of learning they all share. Some of the books are about astronomy and mathematics. Some are about a Lord of Heaven. No missionary has handed them over. No preacher is in the room. They are simply reading, and arguing, and reading again. What they did next is the story. Today: Korea's lay founders.

Among the books, the accounts say, was one written in Chinese by Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit from two days ago, about the Lord of Heaven. The scholars studied it the way they studied everything: closely. One of them, Yi Seung-hun, traveled to Beijing with a mission from the Korean court, found the Catholic church there, and asked to be baptized. He took the name Peter. When he came home, he baptized his friends. And so a church began in Korea led entirely by laypeople, ordinary believers, not clergy. They met in homes, read together, and shared what they learned. For a while they even chose some of their own to lead worship as priests do, until they learned from the bishop in Beijing that only an ordained priest could do that, and they stopped. Acts describes some early believers who "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily". These scholars did something like it, with no priest at their side. It cost them. The faith was soon outlawed, and persecutions came again and again. When a priest finally did arrive, he found a church already there. Catholics in Korea remember these founders and martyrs with honor. Look back at this whole week. Las Casas arguing against conquest. Mary at Guadalupe, in Catholic telling. Martin with his broom, Kateri in the woods, Ricci in scholar's robes, the hidden Christians in Japan. The faith met new peoples in very different ways. Here it arrived as a book, and readers did the rest.
screen: `A BOOK BY RICCI, READ IN KOREA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read, and share what you learn. Sit comfortably, and let the room go quiet. Bring to mind one thing you've learned on this path that stayed with you. A line, a story, a person from this week maybe. Say it to yourself in one sentence, plainly, the way you'd tell a friend at dinner. Then think of who might like to hear it. If you pray, you can pray for that person. If you don't, just hold their name. The bell holds the time.
cheonju. Korean for the Lord of Heaven, the name for God that Korean scholars found in a book from Beijing and used to start a church led by laypeople.
Your line: the laity began it. Today, share your one sentence with that person, in a message or over a meal. Just the sentence, no sermon. Day nine hundred ten.

original.note: cheonju, Korean for the Lord of Heaven, a name for God in Korean Catholic use.

trapdoor: what you thought: missionaries brought Christianity to Korea.
what it means: Korean scholars read Christian books, one was baptized in Beijing, and laypeople began the church.
what a scholar hears: books in classical Chinese, including Ricci's, crossing into Korea, and a lay community writing to the bishop in Beijing to ask what was allowed.

sources.ref: Charles Dallet, Histoire de l'Église de Corée (1874), on the founding
sources.work: history of the Catholic Church in Korea
